questions.q: How is the futur proche built?
choices: Aller in the present, plus an infinitive
Aller in the present, plus de, plus an infinitive
Être in the present, plus an infinitive
questions.why: Je vais partir, nous allons manger. No preposition: je vais à manger is not French.
Aller is conjugated normally and the infinitive follows bare. This is the default future in conversation.
Venir de plus an infinitive is the passé récent. The verb is in the present even though the meaning is past.

questions.q: Where does the negation go in the futur proche?
questions.why: Ne … pas wraps the conjugated verb, which is aller. The infinitive sits outside the sandwich.

questions.q: « Je vais ___ lever. » (I'm going to get up)
questions.why: Pronouns attach to the infinitive, not to aller, and the reflexive pronoun still matches the subject: je vais me lever, tu vas te lever.

questions.q: What is wrong with « Je suis venu de manger » ?
choices: It needs à instead of de
Venir de stays in the present — je viens de manger
Nothing; it means I've just eaten
questions.why: Venir de is a present-tense construction with a past meaning. Putting venir itself into the past produces something French does not say.

questions.q: Which sentence means « I'm going to Paris » rather than a future?
questions.why: An infinitive after aller makes it a future auxiliary; a place after it keeps it a verb of movement. The infinitive is the signal, and the same test sorts je viens de manger from je viens de Paris.
Putting the conjugated verb into the imperfect shifts the whole construction one step back: je viens de → je venais de, I had just.

questions.q: Translate: I was about to leave when he arrived.
a: J'allais partir quand il est arrivé
J'allais partir quand il est arrivé.
questions.why: Aller in the imperfect plus an infinitive is was about to. The interruption is an event, so it takes the passé composé.

questions.q: When should you use « être en train de » ?
choices: Only when the point is that something is in progress right now
questions.why: The ordinary present already covers I am eating: je mange. Être en train de adds insistence on the in-progress-ness, and using it by default makes your French heavy.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I'm not going to see him.
questions.why: Two rules at once: the negation wraps aller, and the object pronoun clings to the infinitive it belongs to.
The pronoun goes between de and the infinitive, because that is where the infinitive's own objects live.

questions.q: « En 2050, les villes ___ différentes. » Which future fits?
questions.why: The futur proche is for the near and planned; a remote, abstract prediction takes the futur simple. Compare attention, tu vas tomber, where only the proche works.

questions.q: Say this out loud: you're going to fall!
questions.why: Imminent and spoken, so the futur proche is the only natural choice here.

questions.q: Place the three constructions on a timeline, and say what each becomes in the imperfect.
a: venir de + infinitive = just happened (je viens de manger) → je venais de manger, I had just eaten. Être en train de + infinitive = happening now (je suis en train de manger) → j'étais en train de manger, I was in the middle of eating. Aller + infinitive = about to happen (je vais manger) → j'allais manger, I was going to eat.
questions.why: All three are a conjugated verb plus an infinitive, and putting that conjugated verb in the imperfect slides the whole thing one step into the past.
